Its roots are in blues, ragtime, European harmony, African rhythmic rituals, spirituals, hymns, marches, vaudeville song, and dance music. Since the 1920s Jazz Age, it has been recognized as a major form of musical expression in both traditional and popular music. Jazz is characterized by swing and blue notes, complex chords, call and response vocals, polyrhythms and improvisation. As jazz spread around the world, it drew on national, regional, and local musical cultures, which gave rise to different styles. New Orleans jazz began in the early 1910s, combining earlier brass band marches, French quadrilles, biguine, ragtime and blues with collective polyphonic improvisation. However,

A good way to move from reference points to a deeper, more personal understanding of what you hear. Listening to Jazz Through Its Periods Jazz history is often presented as a succession of periods, but in practice, these boundaries are never fixed. Styles overlap, ideas circulate, and what seems new in one moment often reappears in another form later on. These periods are better understood as reference points. They help situate the music, but they do not define it entirely. What matters is how they shape the way we listen. Today, everything is available at once. Early jazz, swing, bebop, fusion, and contemporary scenes coexist, waiting to be explored. And that is where this history of jazz becomes useful: not to classify jazz, but to make it easier to contextualize what we are listening to. From there, the next step is simple: start exploring, and let the music guide your choices.

Handy's music career began in the pre-jazz era and contributed to the codification of jazz through the publication of some of the first jazz sheet music. New Orleans origins The music of New Orleans, Louisiana, had a profound effect on the creation of early jazz. In New Orleans, enslaved people could practice elements of their culture such as voodoo and playing drums.[94] Many early jazz musicians played in the bars and brothels of the red-light district around Basin Street called Storyville.[95] In addition to dance bands, there were marching bands which played at lavish funerals (later called jazz funerals). The instruments used by marching bands and dance bands became the instruments of jazz: brass, drums, and reeds tuned in the European 12-tone scale. Small bands contained a combination of self-taught and formally educated musicians, many from the funeral procession tradition. These bands traveled in black communities in the deep south. passages.text: Jazz is often approached through its genres, each of which describes a particular sound, style, or way of playing. But these styles did not appear in isolation. They emerged over time, shaped by musicians, places, and contexts that continuously redefined what jazz could be. Looking at jazz through its periods offers a different perspective. Instead of focusing only on how the music sounds, it helps us understand when and why it sounds that way. From its early development in New Orleans at the beginning of the 20th century to its current global and hybrid forms, jazz has evolved through a series of phases, each marked by distinct musical ideas and cultural shifts. These periods are not rigid categories. They often overlap, and many styles continue to exist long after the moment they first appeared. A bebop record recorded in the 1940s does not carry the same context as one recorded today, even if the language is similar. This is why thinking in terms of periods is not about classification but about context. This article explores the main periods in the history of jazz as reference points. Figures such as Louis Armstrong and King Oliver played a central role in shaping this language. Armstrong, in particular, contributed to a gradual shift toward solo improvisation, placing greater emphasis on phrasing, timing, and individual expression, elements that would become central to later developments in jazz. The Jazz Age: From Local Music to Popular Culture During the 1920s, jazz expanded beyond its regional origins and became widely popular in the United States. This period is commonly referred to as the Jazz Age, a term used to describe both a musical development and a broader cultural moment. This decade is marked by the rapid diffusion of jazz through recordings, radio broadcasts, and the migration of musicians to cities such as Chicago and New York. Jazz became closely associated with urban life, nightlife, and dance, particularly in the context of Prohibition-era clubs. This shift also changed the function of the music. Figures such as Art Blakey and Horace Silver played a key role in shaping this direction. Two Directions, One Foundation Although they are often presented as opposites, cool jazz and hard bop share a common foundation in bebop. Both retain their harmonic complexity and focus on improvisation, but they differ in how they approach expression and structure. Cool jazz tends to favor subtlety and restraint, exploring variations in tone and arrangement. Hard bop, on the other hand, emphasizes energy and immediacy, drawing more directly from African American musical traditions. Rather than representing a break, these approaches illustrate how jazz can evolve in parallel directions, each highlighting different aspects of the same language. This coexistence also reflects broader cultural and geographic differences, particularly between the West Coast and East Coast scenes in the United States. passages.text: | The Origins of Jazz - Pre 1895 A review of New Orleans' unique history and culture, with its distinctive character rooted in the colonial period, is helpful in understanding the complex circumstances that led to the development of New Orleans jazz. The city was founded in 1718 as part of the French Louisiana colony. The Louisiana territories were ceded to Spain in 1763 but were returned to France in 1803. France almost immediately sold the colony to the United States in the Louisiana Purchase. New Orleans differed greatly from the rest of the young United States in its Old World cultural relationships. The Creole culture was Catholic and French-speaking rather than Protestant and English-speaking. A more liberal outlook on life prevailed, with an appreciation of good food, wine, music, and dancing. Festivals were frequent, and Governor William Claiborne, the first American-appointed governor of the territory of Louisiana, reportedly commented that New Orleanians were ungovernable because of their preoccupation with dancing. The colony's culture was enriched not only from Europe but from Africa as well.
